implementation_notes: TypeScript keeps JavaScript's first-class functions and adds the type machinery that makes a combinator library safe to use: `fp-ts` supplies data-last pipeable combinators (`pipe`, `flow`, `Option.map`/`chain`, `Either.mapLeft`/`orElse`/`getOrElse`, `TaskEither` for asynchronous fallible work) together with typeclass instances (`Functor`, `Monad`, `Traversable`), and Effect-style libraries build on the same idea. Composing these retires the class hierarchy for domain logic - a validation or workflow step is a function value with a typed failure - whereas the classic structure stays justified when the DSL must be understood by tooling (decorators, metadata, introspection), because the type-level encodings used here are notoriously hard to read and to explain.
pitfalls: `pipe`/`flow` are ordinary function application: a mis-ordered pipeline still type-checks whenever the types happen to line up, and the compiler cannot see the intent.
Type-level noise: `Either<E, A>` chains produce long inferred types and errors that point deep into the library; annotate intermediate steps to keep diagnostics readable.

Every combinator allocates closures and wrapper objects (`Option`/`Either` boxing); asynchrony needs `TaskEither` or the pipeline ends up as a `Promise<Either<...>>` double wrapper that leaks into call sites.
The library is a dependency surface: upgrading a functional-effect stack touches every module that imports it, so pin versions and keep the DSL boundary small.
